clue.text: Resistant to changing it, bar I am an expert in

indicators.note: 'bar' is the preposition meaning except — all present bar one — so it throws the I out of the word beside it.

parts.note: IT with the I excepted leaves a single letter
the verb comes across as it stands
'an' does the job of 'per' — sixty miles an hour is sixty miles per hour
a pro is the expert, the professional as against the amateur
the setter swaps one linking preposition for the other, the way an expert in a subject is a professor of it

explanation.walkthrough: The comma is the trap: you read 'changing it' as one phrase when the wordplay wants IT with its I barred. Five small pieces, and they arrive in clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: Resistant to changing → TAMPER-PROOF: made so nobody can interfere with it, using the -proof sense of impervious that waterproof and bulletproof carry.

clue.text: See 7
Lesson in speaking presided over by master

indicators.note: to preside is to sit above the gathering, so in a down entry the presiding piece is written at the top.

parts.note: M is the standard abbreviation for master
an oral exam is the one done in speaking rather than in writing

explanation.walkthrough: The schoolmaster of the surface is misdirection twice over: he supplies one letter, and the lesson wanted is the tag at the end of a fable, not an hour on a timetable.
explanation.definitionFit: Lesson → MORAL: the point a fable leaves you with, as in 'the moral of the story' — a lesson drawn from a tale rather than taught in class.

clue.text: Upcoming party to start celebrating Agamemnon's daughter

indicators.note: this entry runs down the grid, so 'upcoming' means the letters are read the other way, climbing back up the column.
to be party to something is to be inside it, taking part in it — so the answer is buried in the words that follow.

parts.note: the seven letters run unbroken backwards across the gap, beginning at the third letter of the first word

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the surface admits to hiding anything, which is the whole art of it — and the Greek princess who avenged her father sits inside a sentence about a party.
explanation.definitionFit: Agamemnon’s daughter → ELECTRA: the Mycenaean princess of Greek tragedy, subject of plays by Sophocles and Euripides and of Strauss's opera.

clue.text: Babe's grub mixed up? Tucking in, girlfriend beginning to eructate

indicators.note: tucking something in is pushing it inside and folding the edges back over it, which is where the two new pieces end up.

parts.note: pied means mottled, mixed in colour — the printer's word for type in a jumble; it opens after two letters
GF is how a girlfriend is abbreviated in a text message

indicators.note: 'beginning to' points at the very start of the word behind it, so only its first letter is taken.

parts.note: the beginning of the doctor's word for belching

explanation.walkthrough: Babe is the film's sheep-herding pig, so the grub is swill. 'Mixed up?' looks like an anagram signal and is really a word in its own right, PIED, waiting to be opened.
explanation.definitionFit: Babe’s grub → PIG FEED: Babe is the pig of the film, so the definition names his dinner by example — what is put in the trough.

clue.text: Open a suggestion

parts.note: overt means done in the open, not concealed
a and one are the same number written two ways

explanation.walkthrough: Three words with no indicator anywhere: the whole difficulty is seeing that 'Open a' is not a phrase but two separate pieces pushed together.
explanation.definitionFit: suggestion → OVERTONE: not a proposal but a hint, the faint extra sense a remark carries — borrowed from the higher notes sounding above a struck string.

clue.text: It's mobilised for deviation and alien subterfuge around America

definitions.text: It's mobilised for deviation and alien subterfuge around America

indicators.note: troops mobilised are called up and marched out of their usual places, which is what happens to every letter here.
'around' says the single letter standing for the country ends up inside the assembly rather than at either end.

parts.note: the fodder — and 'and' is only the joint between the two halves, contributing nothing
A is the crossword's abbreviation for America, the twenty-eighth letter needed

explanation.walkthrough: Twenty-eight letters, and they only add up when you notice that 'and' joins the fodder without belonging to it while 'for' does belong to it. The whole sentence defines as well.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: the federal body mobilised over subversion and foreign espionage inside America, while those same words supply its name.

clue.text: Fancy item of jazz memorabilia on Antiques Roadshow, maybe not particularly presentable?

parts.note: to fancy something is to like it
an unspecified item is a something
in jazz slang a cat is a player; the phrase brings its own 'the' with it
people bring their keepsakes in to the programme to have them valued

explanation.walkthrough: A five-piece charade whose pieces are all ordinary English, which is why it hides so well: the jazz cat really would be bringing something in to be valued.
explanation.definitionFit: not particularly presentable → LIKE SOMETHING THE CAT BROUGHT IN: the idiom for a bedraggled arrival, from the half-dead mouse a cat deposits proudly on the mat.

clue.text: See 6
Cleared by air defence after skirmish, and OK to travel?

indicators.note: clearing a space means carrying away what stands in it, so the letters named are taken out before anything else happens.
a skirmish leaves whatever it touches scattered, so the surviving letters come out in a new order.

parts.note: the fodder, before the deletion
A, N and D come out of it — the little word is doing wordplay, not joining two thoughts

explanation.walkthrough: The word to delete is sitting in the clue looking like plain grammar. Once 'and' has gone, ten letters are seven, and the raid on the surface has nothing to do with it.
explanation.definitionFit: OK to travel → ICE-FREE: said of a port or sea lane that winter has not frozen shut, so shipping can still get through.

clue.text: One drug troublingly Tennyson's reward?

indicators.note: water that is troubled is stirred up and unsettled, so the letters beside the word will not stay as they were given.

parts.note: the seven letters of the fodder, before they are stirred

explanation.walkthrough: Naming a Victorian poet is how a setter warns you that the word is an old one — GUERDON is the poets' term, and no modern sense is coming to rescue you.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson’s reward → GUERDON: an archaic, poetic word for recompense, kept alive by Victorian verse, so the poet's name flags its vintage.

clue.text: Essential for dress colours on outside of uniform?

definitions.text: Essential for dress colours on outside of uniform?

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its middle, so 'Essential' asks for the letter at the very heart of the one beside it.

parts.note: the middle letter of the five in 'dress'

indicators.note: what sits on the outside of a thing goes round it, so the painter's board wraps the single letter.

parts.note: a palette is the board a painter lays the colours out on; it opens after two letters
U is uniform in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: Every word does two jobs at once: the thing really is essential to a dress uniform and really does carry the colours on the outside of one. That double duty is what &lit means.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue defines it: the shoulder piece a dress uniform is not complete without, showing rank and regimental colours on the outside.

clue.text: In Exodus, perhaps, you'll have run through a crowd

indicators.note: a thing driven through another finishes up inside it, which is where the single letter lands.

parts.note: the Authorised Version's word for 'you', which is the English the surface's Exodus is written in
R is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for a run

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb does the defining — two's company, three's a crowd — and 'In Exodus, perhaps' is the setter's polite way of saying: use the Bible's word for you.
explanation.definitionFit: a crowd → THREE: straight out of the proverb 'two's company, three's a crowd', where the number is exactly what makes a gathering one too many.

clue.text: Gold in reserve not often spherical

parts.note: OR is gold in heraldry, and the crossword's usual gold
money put by is money kept in reserve
no letters in this one: it is the setter warning you that the word he wants is a rare one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not often' earns its place by managing expectations — ORBY is poets' English, orb plus an adjective ending, and without the warning you would never trust so short a charade.
explanation.definitionFit: spherical → ORBY: the adjective built from orb, a literary word for round or globe-shaped that survives now mainly in verse and in crosswords.

clue.text: Frantically rang about empty domicile, having been let down — one such?

indicators.note: someone acting frantically does nothing in the order they meant to, and neither do these letters.
an emptied word keeps only its walls, the first and last letters, and loses everything in between.

parts.note: RANG with the D and E that an emptied 'domicile' leaves, shaken together
a tyre that has been let down is flat

explanation.walkthrough: 'One such?' points back at 'domicile', a word the wordplay has already stripped for its outer letters — and 'let down' is the tyre, not the disappointment the surface offers.
explanation.definitionFit: one such? → GARDEN FLAT: the pointer looks back at the clue's own 'domicile', and a garden flat is one — the lower-ground dwelling with the yard behind.

clue.text: With Grace to summon up, ducking delivery?

definitions.note: The answer is an adjective and 'With Grace' is a prepositional phrase; they still swap cleanly, since a movement made with grace is a balletic one. The capital G is the cricketer W. G. Grace, there for the surface alone.

indicators.note: the entry runs down the grid, so 'up' sends the letters of the word before it back the way they came.
to duck is to drop below something, so the turned-round word is written underneath the other piece.

parts.note: a bowler's delivery is a ball
to summon someone to court is to cite them, and CITE is written climbing

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is W. G. Grace ducking a bouncer, and every cricketing word is doing something else: Grace is elegance, summoning is a court's business, the delivery is only a ball.
explanation.definitionFit: With Grace → BALLETIC: describing movement with a dancer's poise and control, the adjective English reaches for whenever an ordinary action looks choreographed.

clue.text: Who say, in fancy dress: 'Can I go as me?'

definitions.text: Who say, in fancy dress: 'Can I go as me?'

indicators.note: at a fancy-dress party nobody turns up as themselves, so the letters arrive in another guise too.

parts.note: the ten letters of the fodder, quoted as if they were speech

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the definition: the only guest who would ask to attend a costume party as themselves is the very thing the letters of that request spell out.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue defines them: people so taken with themselves that they would come to a costume party as themselves, and their question supplies the letters.

clue.text: Slimmers enjoy taking dip

indicators.note: a word that takes something is holding it, so the two words in front are carrying the answer between them.

parts.note: the letters run unbroken across the join, starting two letters into the first word

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'taking dip' as the slimmers' swim and the instruction goes past you: 'dip' is the definition, and the two words before it are the hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: dip → IMMERSE: to dip a thing is to plunge it right under the surface, the verb sense of dip rather than the swim or the thing on a cracker.

clue.text: Such parts this catastrophic?

indicators.note: 'parts' is a verb as well as a noun: to part is to leave, so the five letters it names walk out of the long word.

parts.note: the twelve letters the wordplay works on

explanation.walkthrough: Take PARTS out of CATASTROPHIC and the seven letters left over will not sit still: they spell CHAOTIC, which is also what a catastrophe leaves behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: a catastrophe leaves everything in disorder, and these letters are left in exactly that state once the named ones have departed.

clue.text: Identified with a circle, called, spoke
Absolute idealist turned on by Man

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, so the cricketing word beside it is written from its far end.

parts.note: the pronoun a man answers to
in cricket the on side is the leg side, and those three letters are turned round

explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned on by Man' is deliberately suggestive, and the piece that matters is the cricket sense of 'on'. Absolute idealism is the name Hegel's system goes by.
explanation.definitionFit: Absolute idealist → HEGEL: the German philosopher whose system is called absolute idealism, so the definition names him by the doctrine he founded.

clue.text: What might be refused by statesmen?

definitions.text: What might be refused by statesmen?

indicators.note: read it as re-fused, melted down and run together again, and the letters beside it are free to come out in any order.

parts.note: the nine letters of the fodder

explanation.walkthrough: Two readings of 'refused' at once: politicians turning a policy down, and the letters of 'statesmen' fused together again into something new. The sentence defines as well as builds.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue defines it: the check on income that politicians might vote down, and the very people who would refuse it supply the letters.

clue.text: Selection of exotic cakes along the way gets us high

indicators.note: the letters lie along the words that follow, picked up in order as you travel through them.

parts.note: the five letters run unbroken from the end of the first word into the middle of the last

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the surface owns up to concealing anything: 'gets us high' reads as what the cakes do, and is really the place the answer has been sitting all along.
explanation.definitionFit: Selection of exotic cakes → SUSHI: a platter of the Japanese vinegared-rice cakes, exotic to a British solver and served as an assortment rather than singly.

clue.text: Controversial claim about Glastonbury? One puts the music down

parts.note: the contentious assertion is a flat denial: the words you would use to say the famous hill is nothing of the kind
the Somerset town's landmark is its Tor, the hill with the tower on top

explanation.walkthrough: Standing on Glastonbury Tor and announcing it is not a tor would indeed start an argument — and the definition is the other half of the joke, since putting music down means writing it out.
explanation.definitionFit: One puts the music down → NOTATOR: the person who writes music into notation, setting on paper what has so far only been played or sung.

clue.text: Tortoises originally used to supply cover for Roman soldiers

indicators.note: not the verb but the adverb from supple — pliantly — so the letters beside it will bend into another shape.
'originally' asks for a word at its origin, which is the single letter it begins with.

parts.note: the first letter of the first word
the six letters of 'used to', bent into a new order

explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' as an adverb is one of the language's best traps. The tortoises are not decoration either: the Latin for tortoise is what the legions named this shell of locked shields after.
explanation.definitionFit: cover for Roman soldiers → TESTUDO: the roof of overlapping shields a legion locked overhead when advancing, named from the Latin for tortoise.

clue.text: Cashier's wound dressed with fine designer cravat?

indicators.note: not an injury but the past tense of wind: something wound round has been twisted out of the shape it started in.
a wound is dressed by being bound up with something else, which is how the two sets of letters come together here.

parts.note: the one at the till who checks your goods through is a checker
the four letters join the shuffle exactly as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: The first-aid scene is a lie in every word: 'wound' is the winding sort, 'dressed' is the assembling of letters, and the cashier is at a till rather than bleeding.
explanation.definitionFit: designer cravat → NECKERCHIEF: a square of cloth knotted at the throat, the working cousin of the cravat, which the question mark dresses up as designer wear.
